title: Pointers to Pointers - Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 2e on Pointers to Pointers in CS103, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This lecture covers pointers to pointers in C/C++. The unit is labeled Unit 2e and is part of the CS103 course. Topics include the motivation for using pointers to pointers, passing pointers by reference, pointer type analysis with the address-of and dereference operators, arrays of pointers and their equivalence to 2D arrays, command line arguments using argc and argv, and safe C-string library functions.
notes_text: This is a foundational topic in C/C++ that builds on prior knowledge of single-level pointers. Understanding pointer-to-pointer relationships is critical for dynamic 2D arrays, command line argument handling, and passing pointers by reference to functions.

title: Motivation: Why We Might Need Pointers to Pointers
summary: Section divider introducing the motivation for passing pointers by reference using pointers to pointers.
main_text: This section explores why pointers to pointers are needed in C/C++. The primary motivation is passing pointers by reference, which requires understanding how to modify a pointer variable from within a called function. When a function needs to change the value of a pointer (not just the data it points to), a pointer to that pointer must be passed.
notes_text: This concept extends the familiar pass-by-reference pattern: to modify a variable of type T in another function, you pass a T*. Therefore, to modify a variable of type T* (a pointer), you pass a T** (a pointer to a pointer).

title: Motivation: Finding First and Last Negative Numbers
summary: Introduces the problem of returning two pointers from a function, motivating the need for pointers to pointers.
main_text: Recall finding the first negative number in an array and returning a pointer to it using the function: int* firstNeg(int dat[], int len) which iterates through the array and returns &dat[i] when dat[i] < 0, or NULL if none found. The new challenge is: what if we wanted a function to return a pointer to BOTH the first AND the last negative number? A function can only have one return value, so we need another mechanism. The function signature would be: firstAndLastNeg(int dat[], int len, ___). The example uses int dat1[5] = {14, 8, -3, 2, -9} where ptr1 points to dat[2] (value -3) and ptr2 points to dat[4] (value -9).
notes_text: This slide sets up the core problem: C/C++ functions can only return one value. When multiple outputs are needed, some must be passed as output parameters. Since the outputs here are pointers (int*), the output parameter must be a pointer to a pointer (int**).

images.description: Memory diagram showing an array dat1 at addresses 73a0-73b0 containing values 14, 8, -3, 2, -9, with ptr1 (int*) pointing to dat[2]=-3 and ptr2 (int*) pointing to dat[4]=-9.

title: Solution Using int** for Multiple Pointer Returns
summary: Shows how to use int** parameter to pass a pointer by reference, enabling a function to return two pointers.
main_text: To return pointers to both the first and last negative numbers, we pass one pointer by reference using int**. The function signature is: int* firstAndLastNeg(int dat[], int len, int** lastPtr). Inside the function, firstNeg is tracked as a local int* initialized to NULL. When a negative is found, if firstNeg is NULL it is set to &dat[i]; the last pointer is always updated via *lastPtr = &dat[i]. The function returns firstNeg. In main: int dat1[5] = {14, 8, -3, 2, -9}; int *ptr1, *ptr2; ptr1 = firstAndLastNeg(dat1, 5, &ptr2); The address of ptr2 (&ptr2) has type int**, matching the int** lastPtr parameter. The value at address 7398 is passed for the pointer-to-pointer parameter.
notes_text: The key insight is that passing &ptr2 (the address of an int* variable) gives the function a way to modify ptr2 in the caller's scope. Dereferencing the int** inside the function (*lastPtr = &dat[i]) writes through the pointer-to-pointer to update the caller's ptr2. This is the fundamental pattern for passing any variable by reference in C.

images.description: Memory diagram showing array dat1 at addresses 73a0-73b0, with int* ptr1 at address 7390 containing 73a8, and int* ptr2 at address 7398 containing 73b0, illustrating the pointer-to-pointer relationship.

metadata.topic: Pointers to Pointers for Multiple Returns

title: Recall: A Function to Create an Array
summary: Reviews a function that dynamically allocates and returns an integer array, setting up the next motivation scenario.
main_text: This slide reviews a function that creates and returns a dynamically allocated array. The function ordered_array(int n) allocates an integer array of size n using new int[n], fills it with values 1 to n, and returns the pointer: int* ordered_array(int n) { int* dat = new int[n]; for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) { dat[i] = i + 1; } return dat; }. In main: int* nums = ordered_array(5); iterates to print values, then delete[] nums frees the memory. This works because the function can return the pointer as its single return value.
notes_text: This pattern works when the pointer is the only output. The next slides show a scenario where the function also needs to return a status (bool), which means the pointer must be communicated via a parameter instead of the return value, requiring a pointer to a pointer.

title: Another Scenario: Returning Both Array and Status
summary: Presents a scenario where a function must return both a dynamically allocated array and a boolean status.
main_text: What if we wanted a function to: create an array of size n, fill it with positive integers from the user (via cin), and return a bool indicating whether all numbers are positive? The function getPosUserArray returns a bool for validity and needs to also provide the array pointer back to the caller. The code: bool getPosUserArray(int n, ___) { bool good = true; int* dat = new int[n]; for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) { cin >> dat[i]; if(dat[i] < 0) { good = false; } } *pdat = dat; return good; }. In main: bool ok = getPosUserArray(5, ___); The question is how to pass and receive the pointer to the array.
notes_text: Since the return value is used for the bool status, the pointer must be communicated through a parameter. This requires passing a pointer to the pointer variable (int**) so the function can write the newly allocated array's address back to the caller.

title: Passing Pointers By Reference Using int**
summary: Shows the complete solution for passing a pointer by reference using int** to modify a caller's pointer variable.
main_text: If we want a function to change a pointer in another function, we have to pass the pointer by reference. This implies we need a pointer to a pointer. To change a type T variable in another function, we pass a T*. So if T=int*, we pass T*=int**. The complete solution: bool getPosUserArray(int n, int** pdat) { bool good = true; int* dat = new int[n]; for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) { cin >> dat[i]; if(dat[i] < 0) { good = false; } } *pdat = dat; return good; }. In main: int* nums; bool ok = getPosUserArray(5, &nums); The expression &nums yields an int** which matches the parameter type. Inside the function, *pdat = dat writes the array address into the caller's nums variable.
notes_text: The pattern is universal: to modify a variable of any type T from a called function, pass a pointer to it (T*). When T itself is a pointer type (like int*), T* becomes int**. The dereference *pdat inside the function accesses the original nums variable in main.

title: Passing Pointers By Reference Animation
summary: Animated memory diagram showing stack and heap during pointer-by-reference function call with int** parameter.
main_text: This slide provides an animation showing the sequence of operations when passing pointers by reference. Key points to understand include: where variables and data live in memory (stack vs heap), how long they live, and when they are deallocated. The function getPosUserArray(int n, int** pdat) allocates on the heap with new int[n]. The stack frame for getPosUserArray contains: n (value 5), good (bool), pdat (int** pointing to nums in main), and dat (int* pointing to heap array at 0x4920). The heap contains the array with values {8, 6, 12, 7, 1}. In main's stack frame: nums (int* that receives the heap address via *pdat = dat), ok (bool). The operation *pdat = dat writes through the pointer-to-pointer to set main's nums to the heap array address 0x4920.
notes_text: After getPosUserArray returns, its stack frame (including local dat) is destroyed, but the heap array survives because it was allocated with new. The caller's nums now holds the address of that heap array. The delete[] nums in main eventually frees it. This is a critical memory management pattern.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the stack with two frames (main and getPosUserArray) and the heap. getPosUserArray's frame shows pdat (int**) pointing to main's nums variable. dat (int*) points to heap array at 0x4920 containing {8,6,12,7,1}. Arrow shows *pdat = dat writing the address into main's nums.

metadata.topic: Memory Layout with Pointer to Pointer

title: Review and Syntax Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the review and syntax portion covering pointer-to-pointer declarations and operations.
main_text: This section covers the review of pointer concepts and the syntax for working with pointers to pointers. It builds on prior knowledge of single pointers and extends to multiple levels of indirection, including how to declare, initialize, and use double pointers (int**) and the relationship between the address-of (&) and dereference (*) operators at multiple levels.
notes_text: Understanding the syntax and type rules for pointers to pointers is essential before applying them in practical scenarios like 2D arrays and command line arguments covered later in the lecture.

title: Pointer Analogy with Safe Deposit Boxes
summary: Uses a safe deposit box analogy to explain multiple levels of pointer indirection including int*, int**, and int***.
main_text: We can have multiple levels of pointers (indirection). A box can contain: data, a pointer (reference to another box), or even a pointer to a pointer. Using C/C++ pointer terminology with a numbered box grid: *9 = gold in box 7 (one level: 9 => 7), **16 = gold in box 7 (two levels: 16 => 9 => 7), ***5 = gold in box 7 (three levels: 5 => 16 => 9 => 7). What is stored in one box might be: Box 9 contains a pointer-to an int (int*), Box 16 contains a pointer-to a pointer-to an int (int**), Box 5 contains a pointer-to a pointer-to a pointer-to an int (int***). The grid shows boxes 0-17 with various values, where following chains of references eventually leads to the actual data.
notes_text: This analogy makes the abstract concept of multiple indirection concrete. Each dereference (*) follows one link in the chain. The type tells you how many hops are needed to reach the actual data: int* means one hop, int** means two hops, int*** means three hops.

images.description: Photo of safe deposit boxes alongside a numbered grid (0-17) showing values in each box. Arrows trace the chain: box 5 contains 16, box 16 contains 9, box 9 contains 7, where the gold (data) resides. Color-coded labels show int, int*, int**, int*** types.

title: Pointer Types Distinguish Levels of Indirection
summary: Explains how pointer types (int*, int**) distinguish between different levels of indirection with declaration examples.
main_text: Pointer types help us distinguish between: a pointer to an int (int*), a pointer to a pointer to an int (int**), and so on. Examples: int* p; declares a pointer where an integer is one hop (one level of indirection) away. double **q; declares a pointer where a double is two hops (two levels of indirection) away. Important note: it does not matter if you place the ** next to the type or variable name. The following are the same: double** q; <=> double **q;. The grid analogy continues showing the chain of references with additional type annotations including char and char*.
notes_text: The placement of asterisks in declarations is a matter of style. Some prefer int* p (emphasizing the type is int-pointer) while others prefer int *p (emphasizing that *p is an int). Both are valid. When declaring multiple variables on one line, the * binds to the variable name, not the type, which can cause confusion.

images.description: Same safe deposit box grid as previous slide with additional type annotations showing char and char* types added to the hierarchy alongside int, int*, int**.

title: Operations on Pointers to Pointers
summary: Demonstrates pointer-to-pointer operations with a code example showing declarations, assignments, and dereferences.
main_text: Pointers can point to other pointers, forming a chain of links. Sample sequence: int k, dat[3] = {5, 7, 9}; int *pi; int **ppi; pi = dat; (pi points to dat[0]). ppi = π (ppi points to pi). k = *pi; yields k=5 (dereference pi to get dat[0]). k = (**ppi) + 1; yields k=6 (double dereference: ppi->pi->dat[0], then +1). k = *(*ppi + 1); yields k=7 (dereference ppi to get pi, add 1 for pointer arithmetic to dat[1], then dereference). Important recall: * with a type to the left is declaring a pointer (e.g. int *pi). * with NO type to the left is dereferencing the pointer (e.g. k = *pi). This code is for illustration purposes only.
notes_text: The memory layout shows: dat[0]=5 at 73a4, dat[1]=7 at 73a8, dat[2]=9 at 73ac. pi (int*) at 73b0 holds 73a4 (pointing to dat). ppi (int**) at 73b4 holds 73b0 (pointing to pi). Understanding the difference between declaration * and dereference * is crucial for reading pointer code correctly.

images.description: Memory diagram showing addresses 73a0-73c4 with dat array (5,7,9) at 73a4-73ac, pi (int*) at 73b0 pointing to dat, and ppi (int**) at 73b4 pointing to pi. Arrows show the chain of references.

title: Tip: Finding Your Type with * and &
summary: Provides a systematic tip for determining the resulting type when applying * or & operators to pointer expressions.
main_text: Consider declarations: int k, dat[3] = {5, 7, 9}; int *pi = x, **ppi = π. Note: in declarations, the type (e.g. int) distributes when declaring multiple variables, but the *s do NOT distribute. Tip for figuring out the type a pointer expression will yield: Each * in the expression CANCELS a * from the variable type. Each & in the expression ADDS a * to the variable type. Examples in a table: Given int* pi, expression *pi yields => int. Given int** ppi, expression **ppi yields => int. Given int** ppi, expression *ppi yields => int*. Given int k, expression &k yields => int*. Given int* pi, expression &pi yields => int**. As a sanity check, always ensure the types match on either side of an assignment: x = y; ensure x and y are the same type.
notes_text: This cancellation/addition rule is the single most important mental tool for working with multi-level pointers. It applies universally: if a variable is declared as T with n asterisks, applying m dereferences (*) removes m asterisks, and applying & adds one asterisk. The result must match the type on the other side of any assignment.

images.description: Table showing five rows mapping original type and expression to resulting type: int* pi with *pi yields int; int** ppi with **ppi yields int; int** ppi with *ppi yields int*; int k with &k yields int*; int* pi with &pi yields int**.

title: Check Yourself: Expression Type Exercise
summary: Practice exercise asking students to determine the formal type of various pointer expressions using the cancellation tip.
main_text: Given declarations: int k, dat[3] = {5, 7, 9}; int *pi = x, **ppi = π. Indicate the formal type that each expression evaluates to (int, int*, or int**). Expressions to evaluate: &pi (answer: int**), dat (answer: int*), &k (answer: int*), pi (answer: int*), *pi (answer: int), pi + 2 (answer: int*, pointer arithmetic preserves type), (*ppi) + 1 (answer: int*, dereference ppi to get int*, then arithmetic preserves type), &ppi (answer: int***). It is always a good sanity test to check what type an expression will yield. Ask yourself: are you working apples-to-apples?
notes_text: The tip box reminds students: each * in the expression cancels a * from the variable type, each & adds a * to the variable type. Pointer arithmetic (adding an integer to a pointer) preserves the pointer type. This exercise reinforces the type-checking habit that prevents common pointer errors.

images.description: Table with 8 rows listing expressions (&pi, dat, &k, pi, *pi, pi+2, (*ppi)+1, &ppi) with blank Type column for students to fill in.

title: Understanding Types With & and * Operators
summary: Comprehensive reference showing how & (address-of) adds a pointer level and * (dereference) removes a pointer level.
main_text: The & operator (Address-of): Applying & to a variable of type T yields a type T* result. That is, & adds a * to the resulting type. Examples: int x; => & int => int*. double z; => & double => double*. int *ptr1 = &x; => & int* => int**. double* ptr2 = &z; => & double* => double*. int **ptr3 = &ptr1; => & int* => int**. The * operator (Dereference): Applying * to a variable of type T* yields a type T result. Every * in the expression cancels a * from the type of the variable. Examples: int a = *ptr1; => * int* => int. *ptr2 = 1.25; => * double* => double. *ptr3 = ptr1; => * int** => int*. **ptr3 = 5; => ** int** => int.
notes_text: This slide serves as a comprehensive reference for the two fundamental pointer operators. The symmetry is important: & and * are inverses. Applying & then * (or * then &) returns to the original type. This is marked 'Skip for time' suggesting it is supplementary material for students who want extra reinforcement.

title: Arrays of Pointers Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing arrays of pointers as the other primary reason for using pointers to pointers.
main_text: This section covers arrays of pointers, which is the other primary reason we use pointers to pointers in C/C++. An array of pointers allows us to create an array of arrays (effectively a 2D array) using dynamic memory allocation. This is essential because C++ does not allow dynamically allocating multidimensional arrays directly with new.
notes_text: Arrays of pointers bridge the gap between the limitation of fixed-size multidimensional arrays and the need for dynamically sized 2D data structures. This pattern is used extensively in real C/C++ programs for string arrays, matrices, and image data.

title: Recall: Pointer to Single Variable vs Array
summary: Clarifies that C/C++ syntax does not differentiate between a pointer to a single variable and a pointer to an array.
main_text: C/C++ syntax does NOT differentiate a pointer to a single variable vs. a pointer to an array (it does not have additional syntax for this). Whether int* p points to one int or an array of ints can only be determined based on how the function uses the pointer. Example 1 - pointer to a single variable: void f1(int* p) { *p -= 1; } decrements the integer pointed to by p. Example 2 - pointer to an array: void f1(int* p) { for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { p[i] = 0; } } sets the array pointed to by p to all zeros. The function signature void f1(int* p) is identical in both cases; the semantics differ based on usage.
notes_text: This ambiguity is a fundamental characteristic of C/C++ pointers. The programmer must know from context (documentation, function name, conventions) whether a pointer refers to a single object or an array. This is one motivation for using std::vector or std::array in modern C++, which carry size information.

title: Big Idea: T* is Equivalent to T[]
summary: Establishes the key equivalence that a pointer type T* can represent an array T[], and asks what an array of T* would be.
main_text: In most cases a pointer will be pointing to an array (since the name of an array yields a pointer to it). A char* is equivalent to a char array. For example, char name[6] = "Anika"; means name is a char* (pointing to address 73d8). An int* is equivalent to an int array. For example, int dat[4] = {3,5,8,2}; means dat is an int* (pointing to address 7420). The big question: So what would an array of T* (e.g. T* mat[]) be? An array of pointers, where each pointer points to its own array, effectively creating a 2D array structure. This is the foundation for dynamically allocated multidimensional arrays.
notes_text: The equivalence T* <=> T[] is one of the most important concepts in C/C++. Array names decay to pointers to their first element in most contexts. This means an array of int* (i.e., int* mat[]) is effectively int**, which can represent a 2D array where each row is a separately allocated 1D array.

images.description: Two memory examples: char name[6] showing 'Anika\0' at address 73d8 labeled char*, and int dat[4] showing {3,5,8,2} at address 7420 labeled int*.

title: Multidimensional Arrays Introduction
summary: Introduces the concept of multidimensional arrays for 2D/3D data like matrices and images, indexed by row and column.
main_text: Thus far, arrays have been 1-dimensional (linear) sequences indexed with 1 value (coordinate), such as char dat[6] = {1,2,3,4,5,6};. We often want to view data as 2D, 3D, or higher dimensional data for applications like: matrix data, images (2D or 3D), and data indexed with 2 coordinates (row, col). A 1D array stored in memory is just a linear sequence of bytes at consecutive addresses (e.g., dat at address 7420 through 7426). For images, we can think of data as a 2D grid where each pixel has a row index and column index. The slide shows a grayscale photo being decomposed into individual pixel values in a 2D matrix format with values like 0, 64, 128, 192.
notes_text: Memory is inherently 1-dimensional (linear addresses), so multidimensional arrays must be mapped onto this linear space. Understanding this mapping is essential for working with images, matrices, and scientific data in C/C++.

images.description: Left side shows a 1D array in linear memory at addresses 7419-7426. Right side shows a grayscale photo being decomposed into a 4x4 pixel grid with values (0, 64, 128, 192) representing brightness levels, with Row Index and Column Index labels.

title: Multidimensional Array Declaration and Access
summary: Shows how to declare and access 2D and 3D arrays in C++ with rows, columns, and planes using bracket notation.
main_text: 2D arrays: Declare by providing size along both dimensions (normally rows first then columns) and access with 2 indices. Declaration: int matrix[2][3]; creates a 2-row, 3-column array. Access: my_matrix[0][1] evaluates to 3 (row 0, column 1), my_matrix[1][2] evaluates to 2 (row 1, column 2). 3D arrays: Declare and access data with 3 indices. Declaration: unsigned char image[2][4][3]; creates a 3D array with 2 planes, 4 rows, and 3 columns. Access: image[0][3][1] evaluates to 51. The 3D array can be visualized as multiple 2D planes stacked together (Plane 0, Plane 1, Plane 2), useful for representing color images with separate planes for each color channel.
notes_text: The dimensions in C++ multidimensional array declarations must be compile-time constants. The indexing order is [plane][row][col] for 3D or [row][col] for 2D. Elements are stored in row-major order in memory, meaning the rightmost index varies fastest.

images.description: Two tables: a 2x3 matrix showing values (5,3,1 / 6,4,2) with Row 0/1 and Col 0/1/2 labels, and a 3D array visualization showing three 2x4 planes (Plane 0, 1, 2) with numeric values and Col/Row labels.

title: Limitations of Multidimensional Arrays
summary: Explains that multidimensional arrays require fixed compile-time sizes and cannot be dynamically allocated with new.
main_text: Just like 1D arrays, multidimensional arrays must be declared of a FIXED, constant size and NOT a variable size. Legal declarations: int matrix[2][3]; and unsigned char image[2][4][3]; (all dimensions are constants). Illegal declarations: int matrix[n][m]; and unsigned char image[NX][NY][NZ]; (variable dimensions are not allowed). Also, C++ new CANNOT even dynamically allocate a 2- or 3-D array (for reasons explained in a future unit). Does NOT work: new matrix[n][m]; Does NOT work: new unsigned char[NX][NY][NZ]; But there is a way: Arrays of pointers. The solution is to use many 1D-arrays and an array of pointers to connect them into a logical 2D structure.
notes_text: This limitation is the primary practical motivation for using pointers to pointers (int**) to represent 2D arrays. Since new cannot allocate true multidimensional arrays, the standard C/C++ approach is to allocate an array of pointers (one per row), then allocate each row separately. This is covered in the next slides.

title: Pointers-To-Pointers as 2D Arrays
summary: Shows how an array of pointers (int* mat[4]) creates a 2D array structure, and that mat itself is an int**.
main_text: If a 1D array is known by its starting address (a T* pointer), such as int scores1[5] being an int*, then suppose we had several more integer arrays (scores2, scores3, etc.). An ARRAY of pointers could be thought of as an ARRAY of ARRAYS (i.e. 2D array). For example: int* mat[4]; declares an array of 4 int pointers. An array's type follows T[n] <=> T*, so by substitution with T = int*: int* ptrs[k] implies ptrs is an int**. What would mat be? mat is an int**. The diagram shows mat at address 100, with mat[0]=240, mat[1]=300, mat[2]=480, mat[3]=800, each being an int* pointing to a separate array of 5 zeros (scores1 through scores4), essentially forming a 4x5 2D array.
notes_text: This is the core technique for dynamic 2D arrays in C/C++. Each element of the outer array is a pointer (int*) to a separately allocated inner array. The outer array itself decays to an int** pointer. This structure allows rows to be different lengths (jagged arrays), though typically they are uniform.

images.description: Diagram showing mat (int**) at address 100 with 4 entries (mat[0]-mat[3]) each containing an int* pointer (240, 300, 480, 800) pointing to separate 5-element arrays of zeros, labeled scores1-scores4, forming a 2D array structure.

title: Recall: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays
summary: Reviews the equivalence of array indexing and pointer arithmetic, showing that data[i] is the same as *(data + i).
main_text: Pointer arithmetic and array indexing are really the same! Array syntax vs. Pointer Arithmetic + Dereference syntax: data[i] <=> *(data + i). The programmer writes data[i] and the compiler always converts to *(data + i). The expression (data + i) computes the address of the i-th value in an array. The start address is data, and implicitly i*sizeof_type bytes are added. The * (dereference) operator gets its value. The array brackets [ ] imply dereference (*). Example with data starting at address 7300: data+0=7300 contains data[0]=10, data+1=7304 contains data[1]=11, data+2=7308 contains data[2]=12, through data+5=7320 with data[5]=15. Each int is 4 bytes, so addresses increment by 4.
notes_text: This equivalence is fundamental to understanding how 2D array access works with pointers to pointers. The expression mat[j][k] becomes *(*(mat+j)+k): first dereference mat+j to get the row pointer, then dereference that pointer offset by k to get the element. The compiler handles sizeof scaling automatically.

images.description: Linear array diagram showing 6 elements from data (7300) to data+5 (7320), with both pointer notation (data+i) and array notation (data[i]) labeled, containing values 10-15 at 4-byte intervals.

title: 2D Array Access with Pointer Arithmetic
summary: Shows how mat[j][k] translates to *(mat[j] + k) using pointer arithmetic on an array of pointers.
main_text: An ARRAY of pointers can be thought of as an ARRAY of ARRAYS (i.e. 2D array). With int* mat[4]; we can access elements using 2D syntax: mat[j][k] = 42; is equivalent to *(mat[j] + k) = 42;. The first index j selects which pointer (which row) from the array of pointers. mat[j] dereferences to get the int* for row j. The second index k uses pointer arithmetic to offset into that row's array and dereferences to access the element. The diagram shows the same structure as before with mat as int** pointing to 4 separate row arrays (scores1-scores4), each containing 5 elements.
notes_text: The two-step access pattern is: step 1, mat[j] retrieves the pointer to the j-th row array; step 2, [k] indexes into that row array. This is identical to how a true 2D array works syntactically, but the underlying memory layout differs (scattered rows vs. contiguous memory).

images.description: Same diagram as slide 22 showing mat (int**) with 4 pointer entries pointing to separate 5-element arrays, now with the access expressions mat[j][k] = 42 and *(mat[j]+k) = 42 highlighted.

title: Arrays of Pointers: String Example
summary: Demonstrates the problem of managing multiple related arrays without an array of pointers, using string names.
main_text: We often want to have several arrays of related data, such as storing several text strings (names of contestants). We could declare each array separately, but then we could not use a loop to process them. Example: char name1[8] = "Bill"; char name2[8] = "Anika"; char name3[8] = "Josue"; char name4[8] = "Mei"; To print all names, we must write separate cout statements for each: cout << name1 << endl; cout << name2 << endl; etc. This is labeled as "Painful!" because it does not scale. The memory diagram shows each name as a separate char array at different addresses (73a0, 73a8, 73b0, 73b8), each occupying 8 bytes with the string data and null terminator.
notes_text: Without an array of pointers, each name must be handled individually, making code repetitive and impossible to generalize with loops. This motivates the array-of-pointers solution on the next slide, where a single array holds pointers to all the name arrays.

images.description: Memory diagram showing four separate char arrays (name1-name4) at addresses 73a0-73b8, each 8 bytes, containing strings 'Bill', 'Anika', 'Josue', 'Mei' with null terminators and unused bytes marked as '?'.

title: Pointers-To-Pointers as 2D Char Arrays
summary: Shows how char* names[4] creates an array of pointers to strings, equivalent to a 2D character array (char**).
main_text: Since a char* is the type for a 1D character array (C-String), an array of char* (e.g. char* names[4]) is like an array of arrays, which is a 2D array. The code: char name1[8] = "Bill"; char name2[8] = "Anika"; char name3[8] = "Josue"; char name4[8] = "Mei"; char* names[4] = {name1, name2, name3, name4}; Now we can use a loop: for(int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { cout << names[i] << endl; }. The type of names is char** (the address of the 0-th char* in the array). The diagram shows names (char**) at address 5480, with names[0]=73d0 (pointing to "Bill"), names[1]=73d8 (pointing to "Anika"), names[2]=73e0 (pointing to "Josue"), names[3]=73e8 (pointing to "Mei").
notes_text: The key insight is: type for a 1D char array is char*, and an array of char* gives char**, which is a 2D array of characters. This pattern allows looping over strings, sorting them, or passing them to functions as a single argument. This is exactly how command line arguments (argv) work.

images.description: Diagram showing names (char**) at address 5480 with 4 entries (names[0]-names[3]), each char* pointing to a separate string array ('Bill', 'Anika', 'Josue', 'Mei'), forming a 2D array structure.

title: Arrays of Pointers Memory Layout
summary: Detailed memory layout showing how an array of char pointers (char**) references separate string arrays in memory.
main_text: In essence, we want an array of arrays, but in C/C++ this is usually accomplished as an array of pointers (to the individual arrays). The question: what type is 'names'? The address of the 0-th char* in the array. The address of a char* is really just a char**. The memory diagram shows: name1 at 73a0 ("Bill\0"), name2 at 73a8 ("Anika\0"), name3 at 73b0 ("Josue\0"), name4 at 73b8 ("Mei\0"). The names array starts at 73c0 with: names[0] (char*) = 73a0, names[1] (char*) = 73a8, names[2] (char*) = 73b0, names[3] (char*) = 73b8. The names variable itself is a char** containing the address 73c0.
notes_text: This memory layout clearly shows the two-level structure: the pointer array (names) lives at one location in memory, while the actual string data lives at separate locations. Modifying names[i] only changes which string is referenced, not the string data itself. This distinction is important for understanding pointer swapping vs. data copying.

images.description: Detailed memory map showing addresses 73a0-73dc. Top portion has four 8-byte string arrays (name1-name4). Bottom portion shows the names pointer array at 73c0-73d8, with each entry pointing back to the corresponding string array.

title: Arrays of Constant C-Strings
summary: Shows how const char* arrays point to string literals stored contiguously in memory, using the const qualifier.
main_text: We can have arrays of pointers just like we have arrays of other data types. An array of pointers is most commonly used to create an array of arrays (or 2D array) where each pointer points at a separate array. Using const for string literals: const char *names[4] = { "Bill", "Anika", "Josue", "Mei" }; for(i=0; i < 4; i++) { cout << names[i] << endl; }. The memory diagram shows the strings stored contiguously in memory: "Bill\0" at 73a0, "Ani" continuing "ka\0" at 73a5, "Josue\0" at 73ab, "Mei\0" at 73b1. The names array (char**) at 73c0 contains pointers: names[0]=73a0, names[1]=73a5, names[2]=73ab, names[3]=73b1.
notes_text: When using string literals, the const qualifier is important because string literals are stored in read-only memory and should not be modified. The strings here are stored contiguously by the compiler (not in separate 8-byte buffers), with each starting right after the previous string's null terminator. This is more memory-efficient than fixed-size char arrays.

images.description: Memory diagram showing string literals packed contiguously from 73a0 to 73b4, with byte-level detail including null terminators. The names pointer array at 73c0-73dc points into these packed strings at their respective starting addresses.

title: Command Line Arguments Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing command line arguments as a practical application of char** (arrays of string pointers).
main_text: This section covers command line arguments in C/C++, which is a direct practical application of pointers to pointers. The main function's signature int main(int argc, char *argv[]) uses char *argv[], which is equivalent to char** argv -- an array of pointers to C-strings. This is how programs receive input from the command line without interactive prompts.
notes_text: Command line arguments are one of the most common real-world uses of char** in C/C++ programming. Understanding this section connects the abstract pointer-to-pointer concept to something students use every time they compile or run a program from the terminal.

title: Intro to Command Line Arguments
summary: Compares cin-based interactive input (Method 1) with command line argument input (Method 2) for program data entry.
main_text: Currently, input is obtained using cin (Method 1), which requires human interaction each time the program is run. Example: int main() { int seed; double threshold; cout << "Enter an int and double: "; cin >> seed >> threshold; } invoked as: $ ./prog1 then user types: 42 0.5. But to support scripts (automation) and for other reasons, Method 2 uses command line arguments where data is input on the command line when we launch the application. Example: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { if(argc < 3) { cout << "Not enough inputs" << endl; return 1; } int seed = atoi(argv[1]); double threshold = atof(argv[2]); } invoked as: $ ./prog1 42 0.5 with no interactive prompt needed.
notes_text: Command line arguments enable automation through shell scripts, makefiles, and testing frameworks. The program can be run non-interactively, which is essential for batch processing, CI/CD pipelines, and any scenario where user interaction is impractical.

title: Command Line Arguments: argc and argv
summary: Explains how the OS parses command line input into argc (count) and argv (array of string pointers) for main().
main_text: Now we can understand the arguments passed to the main function: int main(int argc, char *argv[]). At the command prompt we can give inputs to our program rather than querying the user interactively. Example: $ ./prog1 42 0.5 or $ g++ -g app.cpp -o app. The OS processes the command line string, breaking it at whitespaces, and copies each token into individual strings packaged into an array (argv) of pointers to those strings. Each entry is a pointer to a string (char *). argc indicates the length of the argv array. The 0th entry (argv[0]) is always the string containing the program executable name. For $ ./prog1 42 0.5: argc=3, argv=73b0, argv[0]=73d0 pointing to "./prog1\0", argv[1]=73d8 pointing to "42\0", argv[2]=73db pointing to "0.5\0".
notes_text: The OS handles all the parsing and memory allocation for argv. The program receives a pre-built array of C-strings. argv[0] is always the program name, so actual user arguments start at argv[1]. This is why argc is always at least 1 (the program name itself counts as an argument).

images.description: Diagram showing the command line string './prog1 42 0.5' being parsed by the OS into three separate null-terminated strings, with argv array at 73b0 containing three char* pointers (73d0, 73d8, 73db) each pointing to the respective string.

title: Using Command Line Arguments: 3-Step Process
summary: Provides a 3-step guide for using command line arguments: update main signature, check argc, convert strings to numbers.
main_text: Step 1: Update main()'s signature to: int main(int argc, char* argv[]) or equivalently int main(int argc, char** argv). Step 2: Check argc to ensure the user provides enough arguments when they start the program. Remember, the program name is one of the arguments (argv[0]). if(argc < 3) { cout << "Not enough inputs" << endl; return 1; }. Step 3: Use library functions to convert strings to ints or doubles as needed for numeric inputs: atoi() or strtol() for ints, atof() or strtod() for doubles. All are in <cstdlib>. No need to convert text arguments. Complete example: int seed = atoi(argv[1]); // "42" => 42. double threshold = atof(argv[2]); // "0.5" => 0.5. The alternative char** argv notation is equivalent to char* argv[].
notes_text: The strtol() and strtod() functions are preferred over atoi() and atof() because they provide error detection (they can indicate if the conversion failed). atoi() silently returns 0 on failure, which is indistinguishable from a valid input of "0". Always validate argc before accessing argv elements to prevent out-of-bounds access.

images.description: Memory diagram for $ ./prog1 42 0.5 showing argv array at 73b0 with three char* entries pointing to respective null-terminated strings, and argc=3.

title: 3 Types, 3 Actions: How cout Handles char Types
summary: Explains how cout behaves differently for char, char*, and char** types when printing values.
main_text: In this class, it will be helpful to know how cout handles a char, char*, and char**: char: Prints the ASCII character. For example, cout << word[0] prints a single character like 'H'. char*: Loops and prints the entire string (until it finds the NULL character). For example, cout << word prints the full string "Hello". char**: Prints the address stored in the pointer. Like every other pointer-type, cout << &name prints a hex address like 0x460. This is a special behavior unique to char*. For all other pointer types (int*, double*, etc.), cout prints the address. But for char*, cout assumes it points to a C-string and prints the string content instead.
notes_text: This special handling of char* by cout is a common source of confusion. If you actually want to print the address stored in a char* variable, you must cast it: cout << (void*)name; This forces cout to treat it as a generic pointer and print the address rather than the string.

title: 3 Types, 3 Actions Example with cout
summary: Concrete example showing cout output for char (single character), char* (full string), and char** (hex address).
main_text: Given: char word[10] = "Hello"; char *name = word;. The variable word is a char* at address 470 containing "Hello\0". The variable name is a char* at address 460 containing 470 (pointing to word). Three cout examples: cout << word[0] << endl; prints 'H' because word[0] is a char (single character). cout << word << endl; prints 'Hello' because word is a char* (prints the entire string until null terminator). cout << &name << endl; prints '0x460' because &name is a char** (address of the pointer variable, printed as hex address like any other pointer type).
notes_text: Note the terminal output icons showing the actual console results. The key distinction: accessing word[0] yields a single char, word itself decays to char* (string), and &name produces char** (address). These three types trigger completely different behaviors in the << operator.

images.description: Memory diagram showing word (char*) at address 470 containing 'Hello\0', and name (char*) at address 460 pointing to 470. Three terminal output boxes show: 'H' for word[0], 'Hello' for word, and '0x460' for &name.

title: Command Line Argument Exercises
summary: Lists four practice exercises for command line arguments: Cmdargs_sum, Cmdargs_smartsum, Cmdargs_smartsum_str, and toi.
main_text: Practice exercises for command line arguments: Cmdargs_sum (basic summing of command line arguments), Cmdargs_smartsum (smarter version with additional logic), Cmdargs_smartsum_str (string-handling variant), and toi (implementing string-to-integer conversion). These exercises reinforce the concepts of parsing argv, converting strings to numbers with atoi/atof, validating argc, and processing command line inputs in loops.
notes_text: These exercises provide hands-on practice with the argc/argv pattern. The toi exercise likely asks students to implement their own version of atoi, which reinforces understanding of C-strings, character-to-digit conversion, and positional number systems.

title: If Time Section Divider
summary: Section divider for optional supplementary material to be covered if lecture time permits.
main_text: This section contains supplementary material on why pointers to arrays are advantageous, particularly for reordering data efficiently. The following slides compare two approaches to swapping array elements: copying entire arrays (expensive) versus swapping pointers (cheap). This content is covered if time permits during the lecture.
notes_text: The 'If Time' material provides important practical insights about the efficiency advantages of pointer-based data structures. Even if not covered in lecture, students should review this material to understand why pointers to arrays are preferred over copying array data.

title: Why Pointers to Arrays? (1) - Data Copying Approach
summary: Shows the inefficient approach of swapping array data by copying entire strings with strcpy, requiring a temp buffer.
main_text: Suppose we wanted to alter the order of the arrays, changing from "Bill", "Anika" to "Anika", "Bill". One approach: move/swap the data itself using strcpy. The code declares four name arrays and a names pointer array: char *names[4] = {name1, name2, name3, name4};. To swap the first two: char temp[8]; strcpy(temp, names[0]); strcpy(names[0], names[1]); strcpy(names[1], temp);. This copies all bytes of both strings through a temporary buffer. The memory diagram shows the actual string data being moved between the name1 and name2 arrays, with the temp buffer at address 73d8 holding a copy of "Bill" during the swap. This approach could be inefficient for large data.
notes_text: The strcpy approach copies every byte of the string data. For short strings like names, this is tolerable. But for large arrays (e.g., a row of a matrix with thousands of elements), copying all that data is expensive. The next slide shows a much more efficient alternative using pointer swapping.

images.description: Memory diagram showing name arrays at 73a0-73bc with the data being physically moved between arrays during the strcpy swap. Arrows show name1 getting 'Anika' and name2 getting 'Bill'. Temp buffer at 73d8 holds 'Bill' during the operation.

title: Why Pointers to Arrays? (2) - Pointer Swapping Approach
summary: Shows the efficient approach of rearranging data by swapping pointers instead of copying array contents.
main_text: Instead of copying data, we could simply rearrange pointers, which would be independent of the size of the object pointed to and thus quite fast. The code: char *names[4] = {name1, name2, name3, name4}; char* temp = names[0]; names[0] = names[1]; names[1] = temp;. This only swaps the pointer values in the names array: names[0] changes from 73a0 to 73a8, and names[1] changes from 73a8 to 73a0. The actual string data in name1 ("Bill") and name2 ("Anika") remains untouched in memory. The temp variable (char*) at 73dc holds the pointer value 73a0 during the swap. After the swap, names[0] points to "Anika" and names[1] points to "Bill" without moving any string data.
notes_text: Pointer swapping is O(1) regardless of data size -- swapping two 8-byte pointers is the same cost whether they point to 4-character strings or 4-million-element arrays. This is why sorting algorithms on arrays of pointers (like qsort with string comparisons) swap pointers rather than data. This efficiency argument is fundamental to understanding why pointer-based data structures are preferred.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the name arrays unchanged at their original addresses, but the names pointer array at 73c0 now has names[0]=73a8 (pointing to Anika) and names[1]=73a0 (pointing to Bill) after the swap. Only pointer values changed; string data stayed in place.

title: cin/cout and char* Special Behavior
summary: Explains how cin and cout treat char* specially compared to other pointer types, printing/reading strings instead of addresses.
main_text: cin/cout determine everything they do based on the type of data passed. cin/cout have a unique relationship with char*s. When cout is given a variable or expression of any type, it will print the value stored in that exact variable. Exception: when cout is given a char*, it will assume it is pointing at a C-string, go to that address, and loop through each character, printing them out until the NULL character. When cin is given a variable, it will store the input data in that exact variable. Exception: when cin is given a char*, it will assume it is pointing at a C-string, go to that address, and place the typed characters in that memory. Code example: cout << x << endl; // prints 5. cout << dat << endl; // prints 400 (int* prints address). cout << word << endl; // prints Hello (char* prints string). cout << name << endl; // prints Hello. cout << name[0] << endl; // prints H. cout << (void*) name << endl; // prints 440 (cast to print address). cin >> dat; // doesn't work for int arrays. cin >> name; // stores characters starting at address 440.
notes_text: The (void*) cast trick is important: if you ever need to see the actual address stored in a char* variable (rather than the string it points to), cast it to void* first. This overrides the special char* behavior of cout. Similarly, cin >> name is dangerous because cin does not know the size of the buffer and can cause buffer overflows.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int x=5 at address 396, int dat[10] at address 400 (all zeros), char word[10]='Hello' at address 440, and char* name=440 at address 448. Code output comments show what each cout statement prints.

title: C-String Library Vulnerabilities: Buffer Overflow
summary: Demonstrates how strcpy and strcat can cause buffer overflows by writing beyond allocated array boundaries.
main_text: What could go wrong with C-string library functions? Consider the code: char str1[8]; int x = 1; strcpy(str1, "abcdefghij"); strcat(str1, "!");. The problem: str1 is only 8 bytes, but "abcdefghij" is 11 bytes (10 characters + null terminator). strcpy writes past the end of str1, overwriting adjacent memory including the variable x. The memory diagram shows: str1 at address 73a4 (8 bytes: indices [0]-[7]), with x stored immediately after at address 73ac. After strcpy, the characters 'i', 'j', '\0' overwrite x's memory, changing its value from 1 (00000001) to a corrupted value. After strcat appends '!' the null terminator shifts further, corrupting more memory. This is a buffer overflow vulnerability.
notes_text: Buffer overflows are one of the most dangerous security vulnerabilities in C/C++. They can be exploited to execute arbitrary code, crash programs, or corrupt data. This is why the safe versions (strncpy, strncat) with explicit size limits were introduced, as covered in the next slide.

images.description: Three memory state diagrams showing: (1) initial state with str1[8] uninitialized and x=1, (2) after strcpy overflows str1 writing 'abcdefghij\0' past the 8-byte boundary into x, (3) after strcat appends '!' shifting the null terminator further.

title: Safe C-String Library Functions
summary: Introduces safer C-string functions (strncmp, strncpy, strncat) that include a maximum length parameter to prevent overflows.
main_text: The <cstring> library was updated in subsequent versions of C++ to provide safer alternatives to avoid array buffer overflows, with many functions now having a counterpart with 'n' in the name representing a maximum length to read or write. Functions: int strlen(const char *dest) returns string length. int strncmp(const char *str1, const char *str2, size_t num) compares a maximum of n characters. Returns 0 if equal, >0 if first non-equal char in str1 is alphanumerically larger, <0 otherwise. The num parameter should match the length of the shortest input. char *strncpy(char *dest, const char *src, size_t num) copies a maximum of num characters. char *strncat(char *dest, const char *src, size_t num) concatenates a maximum of num characters plus a NULL. See the documentation at https://cplusplus.com/reference/cstring/.
notes_text: The 'n' variants are strongly preferred over their unsafe counterparts (strcmp, strcpy, strcat) in production code. However, strncpy has a subtle issue: if src is longer than num, strncpy does NOT null-terminate the destination. Programmers must manually add the null terminator. The strncat function does add a null terminator after the appended characters.

title: A Stack View of Command Line Arguments
summary: Complete memory/stack view showing how argc, argv, and command line strings are laid out in memory during execution.
main_text: This slide provides a memory/stack view of the command line arguments and the argc/argv arguments passed to main(). For the command: $ ./prog1 4 0.5, the code is: #include <iostream> #include <cstdlib> using namespace std; int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { if(argc < 3) { cout << "Not enough inputs" << endl; return 1; } int seed = strtol(argv[1]); double threshold = strtod(argv[2]); }. The stack layout from top to bottom: thresh (double, 0.5) at 73a0-73a4, seed (int, 4) at 73a8, argc (int, 3) at 73ac, argv (char**, 73b0) at 73b0. The argv array: argv[0] (char*) = 73d0 at 73b4, argv[1] (char*) = 73d0 at 73b8 (actually pointing to different string), argv[2] (char*) = 73d8 at 73bc. Return link at 73c4. The OS section shows the actual string data: "./prog1\0" at 73d0, "4\0" at 73d8, "0.5\0" at 73da.
notes_text: This complete stack view ties together all the concepts: the OS allocates and fills the string data and argv array before calling main. The argc and argv parameters are pushed onto main's stack frame. Local variables (seed, threshold) are also on the stack. The strtol and strtod functions are used here instead of atoi/atof as the preferred safer alternatives.

images.description: Detailed vertical stack diagram showing memory addresses 73a0-73dc with main's stack frame (thresh, seed, argc, argv array entries, return link) and OS section (string data for ./prog1, 4, 0.5). Color-coded labels show variable types and argv pointer relationships.

title: Backup Section Divider
summary: Section divider for backup/supplementary slides at the end of the lecture.
main_text: This section contains backup slides with additional supplementary material. These slides provide extra analogies and examples for students who want additional reinforcement of the pointer-to-pointer concepts covered in this lecture.
notes_text: Backup slides are typically not covered during the lecture but are available as additional study material for students who want more practice or different perspectives on the same concepts.

title: Why Pointers To Arrays: Hotel Room Analogy
summary: Uses a hotel room analogy with four friends in sequential rooms to illustrate arrays as contiguous numbered locations.
main_text: This backup slide uses a hotel room analogy to explain arrays and pointers to arrays. Four friends (Kyle, Gina, Tim, Alice) got sequential hotel rooms numbered 410, 411, 412, and 413. Just like array elements occupy consecutive memory addresses, the hotel rooms are consecutive numbered locations. Each person is assigned to a specific room, analogous to how data values are stored at specific array indices. Knowing the starting room number (410) and an offset lets you find any friend's room, just as knowing the base address of an array and an index lets you access any element. This maps to pointer arithmetic: base_address + index * element_size.
notes_text: The hotel room analogy makes the abstract concept of contiguous memory allocation concrete and relatable. The sequential numbering mirrors memory addresses, and the friends represent data stored at each location. This analogy can be extended: a list of room assignments (an array of room numbers) would be analogous to an array of pointers.

images.description: Illustration showing four cartoon characters (Kyle, Gina, Tim, Alice) each standing above their assigned hotel room (410, 411, 412, 413). Each room is shown as a photo of a hotel room interior, arranged sequentially.
